Issued at 1230 AM CDT Thu Sep 10 2026

Friday - Saturday: Storm Chances Return, Slight Cool Down 

An upper level low is expected to rotate across the western Hudson 
Bay Friday with a longwave upper trough pivoting across the Northern 
Plains and Upper Midwest through Saturday. At the surface, a 
trailing cold front is expected to swing through the Northern Plains 
during the day on Friday. With a surface high departing to the east, 
the pressure gradient will tighten across the Upper Midwest allowing 
for ample return flow and subsequent destabilization through the 
day. Westerly winds on the lee side of the side of the trough axis 
are expected to increase Friday afternoon into Saturday morning, 
helping to introduce plenty of shear across the region. With this 
instability and shear, storms are expected to form in the vicinity 
of the cold front. However, guidance has backed off on the speed of 
this frontal boundary, bringing it through our area by mid Saturday 
morning when there will be little to no instability to work with. 
Guidance as also trended further north with the shear so the 
environment across our area does not look overly conducive for 
severe thunderstorms. Rain showers and sub-severe thunderstorms look 
more likely with the frontal passage at this time with a low chance 
(less than 10%) for a severe storm Saturday afternoon across 
Southwest Wisconsin where the front may not have cleared the area 
just yet. Even though the front that moved through will be a "cold 
front", zonal flow aloft will prevent any significant cool down for 
Saturday with highs still in the mid to upper 70s. 

Sunday - Mid Next Week: Heavy Rain Monday, Much Cooler Mid Week

On Sunday, an upper low over the Pacific Northwest will begin to 
eject to the northeast as a strong ridge builds over the 
Southeastern US. This will lead to a belt of strong southwesterly 
flow over our region for the first half of next week. Moisture 
advection ramps up after the passage of Saturday's cold front but it 
isn't until late in the day Sunday into Monday that the bulk of the 
deeper moisture works its way into the Upper Mississippi Valley. At 
the surface, a warm front is expected to lift north into the area by 
the morning hours on Monday with strong 850 mb moisture transport 
into the frontal boundary. ECMWF pWATs are in the 90th-99.5th 
percentiles with a broad swath of 1.75 inches averaged across the 
area 00Z Monday - 00Z Tuesday. WPC already has most of our area in 
their Day 5 Slight Risk for Excessive Rainfall, indicating a 
potential for heavy rainfall leading to flash flooding. While 
looking at the EFI, the shift of tails or SOT has the area north of 
I-90 highlighted, a similar area to where the NBM has the highest 
probabilities of 2 inches or more rainfall over a 48 hour period 
ending at 7am Tuesday morning. It should be noted that looking at 
the raw NBM data vs the bias corrected NBM data shows a vastly 
differing picture. The raw NBM data is much lower (half an inch to 
almost an inch lower in some places) which seems to be more in line 
with the 09.12Z LREF probabilities. Given the recent wet period 
we've had across the area, its easy to see why the bias correction 
of the NBM is trending a little on the high side. Some of these 
totals will likely be lowered in the coming days but there is still 
a very real chance for a heavy rainfall event that could lead to 
flooding. The pWATs and warm cloud depths will be there but the 
question is whether storms along the boundary will train enough to 
cause a flooding problem. This will be something to keep an eye on 
over the coming days. The soaking rains will also help to knock 
temperatures down quite a bit with highs by mid week likely only 
reaching into the upper 60s to low 70s, much more representative of 
the fall timeframe we're in.
